summary:
kultiv.IA is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers in Junín and Ayacucho, Peru, adapt crop rotation to changing climate conditions. It integrates NASA Earth observation data—including NASA POWER, GPM and MODIS—with regional climate information to provide insights into temperature, precipitation, humidity and land surface conditions.

Using this information, kultiv.IA generates editable, four-season crop rotation proposals through artificial intelligence, allowing farmers to explore alternatives based on their location, previous crops, soil information and water availability. It also provides agricultural calendars, climate monitoring, satellite maps and a conversational agricultural assistant.

By transforming complex Earth observation data into accessible, location-based guidance, kultiv.IA aims to help farmers make more informed decisions, manage climate risks and explore crop rotations that support long-term soil health, water conservation and agricultural resilience.
details:
kultiv.IA: Turning NASA Earth Data into Practical Agricultural Decisions

Farmers in the Andean regions of Peru face increasing uncertainty when deciding what to plant, when to plant it, and how to manage their land across successive agricultural campaigns. Changing rainfall patterns, temperature variations, and limited access to understandable climate information can make crop planning difficult. Access to data alone is not enough: farmers need practical tools that help translate environmental information into informed agricultural decisions.

kultiv.IA is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform designed for farming communities in Junín and Ayacucho, Peru. It brings together NASA climate and Earth science products, regional agricultural references, farmer-provided information, and artificial intelligence to support crop rotation planning and climate-aware agricultural decisions.

1. How kultiv.IA uses NASA and climate data

When a farmer selects a district or populated area, the platform retrieves and organizes regional environmental information from several sources:

  • NASA POWER: Provides daily temperature, minimum temperature, precipitation, and relative humidity indicators. Solar radiation is also queried when available.
  • NASA POWER Hydrology: Provides a modeled root-zone moisture index (GWETROOT) and regional land evaporation estimates (EVLAND), offering additional environmental context.
  • NASA GPM IMERG: Supplies historical satellite-based precipitation information, aggregated by month through NASA POWER.
  • NASA MODIS through GIBS: Provides a daytime land-surface-temperature layer that farmers can explore on the interactive map.
  • Historical climate references: Monthly averages and comparisons with the same months in the five previous complete years help users explore regional climate patterns.
  • Short-term weather information: The platform displays forecast information through wttr.in and provides access to official SENAMHI forecast and warning resources for complementary consultation.

Together, these sources help farmers understand regional climate conditions and historical variability rather than relying exclusively on isolated weather observations.

2. Main platform functionalities and strengths

  1. Regional Climate Dashboard

Displays available temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, solar radiation, modeled root-zone moisture, and land evaporation indicators for the selected area.

Strength: Brings multiple environmental variables together in one accessible interface, helping users understand the broader climate context relevant to agricultural planning.

  1. Historical Climate Monitoring

Presents monthly climate averages for the current year and historical references based on the five previous complete years, when sufficient data are available.

Strength: Helps farmers explore recurring seasonal patterns and compare current conditions with historical references. These comparisons are contextual information, not guaranteed predictions of future weather.

  1. AI-Powered Crop Rotation Planner

Combines regional climate indicators and agricultural references with information farmers can provide, such as previous crops, soil conditions, and water availability. Using Groq, the system generates a structured proposal of four crops across four agricultural campaigns.

The generated sequence is validated, consecutive crop repetitions are rejected, and the farmer can review, modify, and save the proposed plan.

Strength: Converts environmental information into an editable planning option instead of leaving farmers with disconnected climate figures or a fixed recommendation.

  1. Agricultural Calendar

Allows farmers to explore crop, location, month, and water availability. It presents regional sowing references, historical climate information, and short-term forecast information when available.

The platform includes references for crops such as potato, maize, broad bean, and quinoa.

Strength: Connects crop selection and planting decisions with local agricultural references and environmental context.

  1. Interactive Agricultural Map

Combines geographic information, street maps, satellite imagery, sowing reference points, and the NASA MODIS daytime land-surface-temperature layer. Users can select the area and explore available map dates and layers.

Strength: Makes geographic and environmental information easier to visualize and understand.

  1. Conversational Agricultural Assistant

Uses Groq-powered AI to answer farmers' questions using the selected location and available agricultural context. It also includes basic alternative responses if the AI service is unavailable.

Strength: Makes information more accessible through natural-language interaction, reducing the need for users to interpret technical datasets on their own.

3. How this can make a difference for farmers

The potential impact of kultiv.IA lies in connecting information with action.

A farmer can explore regional rainfall and temperature patterns, consider available information about their previous crop and water conditions, review a proposed crop sequence, and adjust the plan according to their knowledge and local advice.

This process aims to support:

  • More informed crop planning: Farmers can consider environmental conditions and historical climate patterns before selecting crops.
  • Better-informed rotation decisions: The four-campaign planner offers alternative crop sequences that farmers can review rather than relying only on intuition or repeating familiar choices.
  • Greater climate awareness: Historical references and available weather information help users recognize regional patterns and uncertainty.
  • More responsible resource planning: Climate and hydrological indicators provide additional context when considering water availability and agricultural management.
  • More accessible agricultural information: An interactive interface and conversational assistant help bring complex environmental information closer to farming communities.

We do not claim that kultiv.IA has already increased crop yields, reduced water consumption, or improved soil health. These outcomes must be demonstrated through field validation. Our next step is to work with local farmers and agricultural specialists to assess the usefulness of the recommendations, monitor changes in crop-planning decisions, and evaluate adoption across agricultural campaigns. Longer-term evaluation should also examine crop diversity, productivity, soil indicators, and water management.

4. Technology, innovation, and vision

kultiv.IA was developed using React and JavaScript for the frontend, Python and FastAPI for the backend, Leaflet for interactive mapping, and Groq for AI-powered agricultural assistance and crop rotation proposals.

Its innovation is not simply the use of artificial intelligence or satellite data independently. It is the integration of regional climate information, farmer-provided agricultural context, interactive visualization, and editable AI-generated crop rotation proposals into one practical decision-support workflow.

The platform is designed to support farmers, not replace their knowledge or the expertise of agricultural specialists. Its geographic and climate information is regional and approximate; it does not automatically measure individual field conditions or determine the agronomic suitability of a specific plot.

Our vision is to make Earth science information useful at the farm-planning level: helping rural communities understand their changing environment, explore better-informed crop rotation options, and build greater resilience to climate variability.
